label: Th2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Th2}Let $\varphi_{\circ}\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ denotes the normalized
eigenvector for $\lambda_{\circ}\in\sigma(K_{0})\backslash\left\{  0,-1/2\right\}
$. There exists $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ and a unique couple of functions
$(0,\varepsilon_{0})\ni\varepsilon\mapsto\kappa_{\pm}\left(  \varepsilon
\right)  $, analytic with respect to $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, such that:\medskip
\newline$i)$ if $\rho_{0}/\lambda_{\circ}<0$, then
\[
\kappa_{\pm}(  \varepsilon)  =\pm\sqrt{2}\,\left\vert \frac
{{\rho_{0}}}{\lambda_{\circ}}\right\vert ^{1/2}
\Vert\varphi_{\circ}\Vert_{\hat{H}^{-1/2}(\Gamma)}
\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\left(  1+{O}(\varepsilon
)\right)  +{O}(  \varepsilon^{2})
\]
and $\kappa_{\pm}^{2}(  \varepsilon)  $ are both resonances of
$L(\varepsilon)$;
\medskip\newline$ii)$ if $\rho_{0}/\lambda_{\circ}>0$, then
\[
\kappa_{\pm}(\varepsilon)=\pm i\sqrt{2}\,\left(  \frac{{\rho_{0}}}{\lambda
_{\circ}}\right)  ^{1/2}\Vert\varphi_{\circ}\Vert_{\hat{H}^{-1/2}(\Gamma)} 
\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\left(  1+{O}(\varepsilon)\right)  +{O} 
\left(  \varepsilon^{2}\right)
\]
and $\kappa_{+}^{2}(  \varepsilon)  $ is a negative eigenvalue,
while $\kappa_{-}^{2}(  \varepsilon)  $ is a resonances of
$L(\varepsilon)$.

body_md:
\label{Remark_inverse}If 
\[
d_{\ell}=d_{\circ}\in\mathbb{R}\backslash\left\{  -1,0\right\}  \quad\forall
\ \ell=1,...,n\,,
\]
in particular, if $\Omega$ is made of a single connected component, then assumption \emph{H0} rephrases as 
$$
\text{$\mu^{-1}(  d_{\circ})
\notin\sigma(  K_{0})  $ or $\mu^{-1}(  d_{\circ})
\in\sigma(  K_{0})  $ is a simple eignvalue.}
$$
head: environment

label: Theorem_inverse
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\kappa\mapsto(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  $ is
analytic and $\kappa\mapsto\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa}$ compact-operator
valued, the meromorphic Fredholm theory applies, see \cite[Theorem
XIII.13]{ReSi IV}. Hence, either the map (\ref{Op_pencil_inv}) is finitely
meromorphic in $\mathbb{C}$ or $(1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})$ is
nowhere invertible. We distinguish the two cases: 1) $1\notin\sigma\left(
\mu(  d)   K_{0}\right)  $; 2) $1\in\sigma\left(  \mu\left(
d\right)   K_{0}\right)  $ is a simple eigenvalue.

1) If $1\notin\sigma\left(  \mu(  d)   K_{0}\right)  $, then
$\ker\left(  1-\mu(  d)   K_{0}\right)  =\varnothing$. Hence
$(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  ^{-1}\in\mathscr{B} 
(H^{-1/2}(\Gamma))$ exists by the Fredholm alternative and, by continuity of
$\kappa\mapsto(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  $, the
operators $(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  ^{-1} 
\in\mathscr{B}(H^{-1/2}(\Gamma))$ exist in an open neighbourhood of $\kappa=0$.
Henceforth (\ref{Op_pencil_inv}) is finitely meromorphic in $\mathbb{C}$.

2) Let $1\in\sigma\left(  \mu(  d)   K_{0}\right)  $ be simple and
assume that $(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  $ is not
invertible at any $\kappa\in\mathbb{C}$. We show that this statement leads to
a contradiction. By the Fredholm alternative, $\ker\left(  1-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,K_{\kappa}\right)  \neq\left\{  0\right\}  $, which is equivalent
to say that, for each $\kappa$, there exists a non-trivial solution
$\varphi(\kappa)\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ of the eigenvalue problem 
\[
\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa}\varphi(\kappa)=\varphi(  \kappa)
\,.
\]
We work in a disk ${D}_{\delta}$ with $\delta>0$ small and denote 
\[
{D}_{\delta}^{+}:=\left\{  \kappa\in\mathbb{C}_{+}:\left\vert \kappa
\right\vert <\delta\right\}  \,.
\]
Since $\kappa\mapsto\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa}$ is analytic and
$1\in\sigma\left(  \mu(  d)   K_{0}\right)  $ is not-degenerate,
the Kato-Rellich theorem applies (e.g. \cite[Theorem XII.8]{ReSi IV}).
Therefore, the eigencouple $(1,\varphi(  \kappa)  )$ is analytic in
$D_{\delta}$. Let us define $\psi(\kappa):=S\!L_{\kappa}\varphi(\kappa)$. By
the trace maps properties of the single-layer operator, one gets
\begin{equation}
\left[  \gamma_{0}\right]  \psi(\kappa)=0\,,\qquad\left[  \gamma_{1}\right]
\psi(\kappa)=-\varphi(  \kappa)  =-\mu(  d)
\,\gamma_{1}\psi(\kappa)\,. \label{transmission_bc_id} 
\end{equation}
For $\kappa\in{D}_{\delta}^{+}$, the well-known mapping properties (see e.g.
in \cite[Theorem 6.12 and successive remarks]{McLe}), the first jump condition
in (\ref{transmission_bc_id}) and the identity 
\begin{equation}
-\Delta S\!L_{\kappa}\varphi(\kappa)|\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash\Gamma=\kappa^{2}S\!L_{\kappa}\varphi
(\kappa)|\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash\Gamma\,,\label{SL_id} 
\end{equation}
imply $\psi(\kappa)\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\cap L_{\Delta}^{2}(\mathbb{R} 
^{3}\backslash\Gamma)$. Define $L_{1,d}$ as in (\ref{L_cd_def})-(\ref{L_d_dom})
with $c_{\ell}=1$ for all $\ell$ and $d=\left(  d_{1},...d_{\ell}\right)  $.
Then, (\ref{transmission_bc_id}) corresponds to the boundary conditions
(\ref{transmission_bc}). It follows that $\psi(\kappa)\in\mathcal{D}_{d}$ and,
using (\ref{L_cd_def}) and (\ref{SL_id}), one obtains 
\[
L_{1,d}\psi(\kappa)|\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}=\kappa^{2} 
\psi(\kappa)|\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}\,,\qquad L_{1,d} 
\psi(\kappa)|\Omega_{\ell}=\kappa^{2}d_{\ell}\psi(\kappa)|\Omega_{\ell}\,.
\]
Therefore, for any $\kappa\in{D}_{\delta}^{+}$, one gets the identities 
\begin{align*}
\left\langle \psi(\kappa),L_{1,d}\psi(  \kappa)  \right\rangle
_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}=  &  \left\langle \psi(\kappa),-{\Delta}\psi
(\kappa)\right\rangle _{L^{2}(\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})}+ 
                                        
               
{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{\ell=1}^{n}}
             
\left\langle \psi(  \kappa)  ,-d_{\ell}\,{\Delta}\psi
(\kappa)\right\rangle _{L^{2}(\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }\\
=  &  \kappa^{2}\left(  \left\Vert \psi(\kappa)\right\Vert _{L^{2}(\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }^{2}+ 
                                        
               
{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{\ell=1}^{n}}
             
d_{\ell}\,\left\Vert \psi(\kappa)\right\Vert _{L^{2}(  \Omega_{\ell
})  }^{2}\right)
\end{align*}
and 
\begin{align*}
\left\langle L_{1,d}\psi(\kappa),\psi(  \kappa)  \right\rangle
_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}=  &  \left\langle -{\Delta}\psi(\kappa),\psi
(\kappa)\right\rangle _{L^{2}(  \Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }+ 
                                        
               
{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{\ell=1}^{n}}
             
\left\langle -d_{\ell}\,{\Delta}\psi(  \kappa)  ,\psi
(\kappa)\right\rangle _{L^{2}(  \Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }\\
=  &  \overline{\kappa^{2}}\left(  \left\Vert \psi(\kappa)\right\Vert
_{L^{2}(  \Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }^{2}+ 
                                        
               
{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{\ell=1}^{n}}
             
d_{\ell}\,\left\Vert \psi(\kappa)\right\Vert _{L^{2}(  \Omega_{\ell
})  }^{2}\right)  \,.
\end{align*}
Since $\varphi(\kappa)\neq0$, from the injectivity of $S\!L_{\kappa}$ there
follows $\psi(  \kappa)  \neq0$ for any $\kappa$. For $\kappa\in
{D}_{\delta}^{+}\backslash i\mathbb{R}_{+}$, one has $\kappa^{2}\neq
\overline{\kappa^{2}}$ and the symmetry of $L_{1,d}$ (as an operator in
$L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$) implies 
\begin{equation}
\left\Vert \psi(  \kappa)  \right\Vert _{L^{2}(
\Omega_{\mathrm{ex}})  }^{2}+ 
                                        
               
{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{\ell=1}^{n}}
             
d_{\ell}\,\left\Vert \psi(  \kappa)  \right\Vert _{L^{2}(\Omega
)}^{2}=0\,. \label{abv} 
\end{equation}
By (\ref{d_sign_ass}), there exists $d_{\ell_{\circ}}<0$ for some $\ell_{\circ}$.
Choosing ${D}_{\delta}\ni\kappa_{\circ}>0$ and taking the limit ${D}_{\delta} 
^{+}\backslash i\mathbb{R}_{+}\ni\kappa\rightarrow\kappa_{\circ}$ in (\ref{abv}),
one gets 
\[
\Vert \psi(\kappa_{\circ})\Vert _{L^{2}(\Omega_{\+})  }^{2}\leq\vert d_{\ell_{\circ} 
}\vert\,\Vert \psi(\kappa_{\circ})\Vert _{L^{2}(\Omega_{\tilde{\ell}})  }^{2}\,.
\]
Hence, $\psi(\kappa_{\circ})\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$. Let $r>0$ such that
$\Omega\subset B_{r}$; by (\ref{SL_id}), $\psi_{\circ}(\kappa_{\circ})$ solves the
Helmholtz equation outside $B_{r}$; the Rellich estimate implies $\left.
\psi(\kappa_{\circ})\right\vert B_{r}=0$ (see, e.g., \cite[Corollary 4.8]{Leis}).
Then, by the unique continuation property, $\left.  \psi\left(  \kappa
_{\circ}\right)  \right\vert \Omega_{\mathrm{ex}}=0$. Since
$\psi\left(  \kappa_{\circ}\right)  $ fulfills (\ref{transmission_bc_id}), both
the inner traces $\ $at $\Gamma$, $\gamma_{j}^{\mathrm{in}}\psi\left(
\kappa_{\circ}\right)  $, $j=0,1$, vanish. From (\ref{SL_id}) there follows 
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}
[c]{l} 
\left(  \Delta+\kappa^{2}\right)  \psi(\kappa_{\circ})|\Omega=0\,,\\
\gamma_{0}^{\mathrm{in}}\psi(\kappa_{\circ})=\gamma_{1}^{\mathrm{in}}\psi
(\kappa_{\circ})=0\,.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
This implies $\left.  \psi(\kappa_{\circ})\right\vert \Omega=0$. In conclusion,
$\psi(\kappa_{\circ})=S\!L_{\kappa}\varphi(\kappa_{\circ})=0$, which is in
contradiction with $\varphi(\kappa_{\circ})\neq0$.

label: dom_id
title: Lemma

label: transmission_bc_global
title: Proof
body_md:
If $u\in\mathcal{D}_{d}$ then $u\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\cap L_{\Delta} 
^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash\Gamma)$; by $L_{\Delta}^{2}(\mathbb{R} 
^{3}\backslash\Gamma)\equiv{\mathrm{dom}}(\Delta_{\Omega_{\+}}^{\mathrm{max}}\oplus\Delta_{\Omega}^{\mathrm{max}})$, for
$\operatorname{Im}\kappa>0$ one has (see \cite[Lemma 4.2]{MaPoSi JDE 2016})
\[
u=u_{\circ}+S\!L_{\kappa}\varphi-D\!L_{\kappa}\phi\,,\qquad u_{\circ}\in
H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\,,\ \varphi\in H^{-3/2}(\Gamma)\,,\ \phi\in
H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)\,.
\]
The boundary conditions (\ref{transmission_bc}), corresponding to 
\begin{equation}
\lbrack\gamma_{0}]u=0\,,\qquad\left[  \gamma_{1}\right]  u=-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,\gamma_{1}u\,, \label{transmission_bc_global} 
\end{equation}
imply $\phi=0$ and $\varphi=\mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1}u$. This gives
\[
u=u_{\circ}+\mu(  d)  \,S\!L_{\kappa}\gamma_{1}u\,,
\]
where $\gamma_{1}u$ is determined, for any fixed $u_{\circ}$, by the boundary
equation 
\[
(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  \gamma_{1}u=\gamma
_{1}u_{\circ}\,.
\]
For $\kappa\in\Sigma_{d}$ there follows 
\[
\gamma_{1}u=(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  ^{-1} 
\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}\,,
\]
which leads to 
\begin{equation}
u=u_{\circ}+S\!L_{\kappa}^{-1}(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})
\mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}\,. \label{dom_shape} 
\end{equation}
Conversely, if $\kappa\in\Sigma_{d}\cap\mathbb{C}_{+}$ and $u$ is defined by
(\ref{dom_shape}) with $u_{\circ}\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$, then $u\in
H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\cap L_{\Delta}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash\Gamma)$ (by
the single-layer mapping properties) and, by taking the Neumann trace of
(\ref{dom_shape}), one has 
\[
\gamma_{1}u=\left(  1+S\!L_{\kappa}\left(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa
}\right)  \mu(  d)  \right)  \,\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}\,.
\]
Then, by 
\begin{align*}
&  \left.  \left[  \gamma_{1}\right]  u=-\left(  1-\mu(  d)
\,K_{\kappa}\right)  \mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}=-(1-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,K_{\kappa}+\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})\left(  1-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,K_{\kappa}\right)  ^{-1}\mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1} 
u_{\circ}\right. \\
&  \left.  -(  1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa})  \left(
1-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa}\right)  ^{-1}\mu(  d)
\,\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}-\mu(  d)  \,K_{\kappa}^{-1}\left(  1-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,K_{\kappa}\right)  \mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1}u_{\circ}\right.
\\
&  \left.  -\mu(  d)  \,(\left(  1-K_{\kappa}\left(  1-\mu\left(
d\right)  \,K_{\kappa}\right)  ^{-1}\mu(  d)  \right)  \gamma
_{1}u_{\circ}\right.
\end{align*}
there follows $u\in\mathcal{D}_{d}$.

label: Theorem_zero_eigenvalue
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Theorem_zero_eigenvalue} If $d_{\ell}=d_{\circ}\in(-\infty,0)\backslash\{  -1\}$
 for any index $\ell$ and $\mu(  d_{\circ})^{-1}  \in\sigma(K_{0})$, then $0\in\sigma_{p}(L_{c,d})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For brevity, we use the notation $\lambda_{\circ}\equiv\mu(
d_{\circ}) ^{-1}\in\sigma(  K_{0}) $. Given $\varphi_{\circ}\in\ker(  \lambda_{\circ}- K_{0})\backslash\{0\}  $, let $u_{0}:=S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}$. One has $\Delta_{\Omega}(u_{0}|\Omega)=0$, $\Delta_{\Omega_{\+}}(u_{0}|\Omega_{\+})=0$ and, by the jump properties of the single layers, 
$$
[  \gamma_{0}]  u_{0}=0\,,
\qquad
[  \gamma_{1}]  u_{0}=-\varphi_{\circ}=-\lambda_{\circ}^{-1}K_{0}\varphi_{\circ}=-\lambda_{\circ}^{-1}\gamma_{1}S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}=-\lambda_{\circ}^{-1}u_{0}\,.
$$
Therefore, by (\ref{L_cd_def}) and (\ref{transmission_bc}),  if  $u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb R^{3})$ then $u_{0}\in\text{\rm dom}(L_{c,d})$ and $L_{c,d}u_{0}=0$  (hence, $0\in\sigma_{p}(L_{c,d})$) .
\par
Since $\varphi_{\circ}\in H^{-1/2}(  \Gamma)  $,  one has
$\chi_{B_{r}}S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\in H^{1}(  \mathbb{R}^{3})$ for any $r>0$; to conclude we need
to prove that $\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\in H^{1}(  \mathbb{R}^{3})  $ for $r$ large enough. In the following we take $r>0 $ so that $\Omega\subset\subset B_{r}$. Defining $\hat x:={x}/{|x|}$, one has
$$
\frac{1}{|x-y| }=
\frac{1}{| x|}\,\frac{1}{| \hat{x}-y/| x|\,| }=\frac{1}{| x|}\left(1+\int_{0}^{1/|x|}\frac{(\hat x-sy)\cdot y}{|\hat x-sy|^{3}}\,ds\right)=
\frac{1}{| x|}+\frac{h(x,y)}{| x|^{2}}\,,
$$
$$
h(x,y):=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\hat x-sy/|x|\,)\cdot y}{|\hat x-sy/|x|\,|^{3}}\,ds\,.
$$
Similarly, defining $\widehat{x-y  }:={(x-y)  }/{| x-y|}$, one has
\begin{align*}
\nabla_{\!x}\,\frac{1}{| x-y| }=&\frac{\widehat{x-y  }}{| x-y| ^{2}}=\frac{\widehat{
x-y  }}{|x| ^{2}}\,\frac{1}{| \hat x-y/|x|\, | ^{2}}=\frac{\widehat{
x-y  }}{|x| ^{2}}\left(1+2\int_{0}^{1/|x|}\frac{(\hat x-sy)\cdot y}{|\hat x-sy|^{4}}\,ds\right)\\
=&\left(
\frac{1}{|x|^{2}}+\frac{\tilde h(x,y)}{|x|^{3}}\right)\widehat{x-y  }\,,
\end{align*}
$$
\tilde h(x,y):=2\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(\hat x-sy/|x|\,)\cdot y}{|\hat x-sy/|x|\,|^{4}}\,ds\,.
$$
This entails, for any $\varphi$ sufficiently regular,
\begin{align*}
\left(  \chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}S\!L_{0}\varphi\right)  (
x)  
= \frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x| }\int_{\Gamma}\varphi(  y)\,d\sigma_{\Gamma}(y)
+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{2} }\int_{\Gamma}h(x,y)
\varphi(  y)\,d\sigma_{\Gamma}(y)
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
\left(  \chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}\nabla S\!L_{0}\varphi\right)  (
x)  =\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{2} }\int_{\Gamma}(\widehat{x-y  })\varphi(  y)\,d\sigma_{\Gamma}(y)
+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{3} }\int_{\Gamma}\tilde h(x,y)(\widehat{x-y  })\varphi(  y)\,d\sigma_{\Gamma}(y)\,.
\end{align*}
Therefore (notice that $\widehat{x-(\cdot)}$, $h(x,\cdot)$ and $\tilde h(x,\cdot)$ belong to $\mathcal C^{1}(\Gamma)$ whenever $x$ is far away from $\Omega$), 
\begin{align*}
|\left(  \chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\right)  (
x)|^{2}\lesssim &\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{2} }\ \big|\langle1,\varphi_{\circ}\rangle_{\frac12,-\frac12}\big|^{2}+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{4} }\, \sup_{|x|>r}\|h(x,\cdot)\|_{\frac12}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}
\\
\lesssim &\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{2} }\ \big|\langle1,\varphi_{\circ}\rangle_{\frac12,-\frac12}\big|^{2}+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{4} }\, \sup_{|x|>r}\|h(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
&|\left(  \chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}\nabla S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\right)  (
x)|^{2}\\
\lesssim &\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{4} }\ 
\, \sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\|_{\frac12}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}
+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{6} }\,\sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\tilde h(x,\cdot)\|_{\frac12}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}
\\
\lesssim &\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{4} }\ 
\, \sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\|_{1}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}
+\frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{6} }\,\sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\tilde h(x,\cdot)\|_{1}\|\varphi_{\circ}\|_{-\frac12}\,.
\end{align*}
Let us recall that 
\begin{equation}\label{due}
\langle 1,\varphi\rangle_{\frac12,-\frac12}=[S_{0}^{-1}1,\varphi]_{-\frac12}\,,
\end{equation}
where $[\cdot,\cdot]_{-\frac12}$ denotes the scalar product in $H^{-\frac12}(\Gamma)$ with respect to which $K_{0}$ is self-adjoint and  that $S_{0}^{-1}1$ is the eigenvector of $K_{0}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $-\frac12$.  
Since $d_{\circ}\not=-1$,  for the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\circ}$ there holds $\lambda_{\circ}=-\frac12 $ and so the eigenfunction $\varphi_{\circ}$ is always orthogonal to $S_{0}^{-1}1$. Moreover, 
$$
\sup_{| x|>r}\|h(x,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}(\Gamma)}<+\infty\,,\quad \sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\|_{H^{1}(\Gamma)}<+\infty\,,\quad \sup_{|x|>r}\|\widehat{x-(\cdot)}\tilde h(x,\cdot)\|_{H^{1}(\Gamma)}<+\infty\,.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(x)\left(|\left(  S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\right)  (
x)|^{2}+|\left(  \nabla S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\right)  (
x)|^{2}\right)\lesssim \frac{\chi_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\backslash B_{r}}(  x)  }{|x|^{4} }
$$
and the proof is done.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\psi\in\mathcal{C}_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ such that $\psi
|U_{1}\cup U_{2}=1$. Then, by $S\!L_{k}=R_{k}\gamma_{0}^{\ast}$, by
$\gamma_{0}^{\ast}\in\mathscr{B}(H^{-1/2}(\Gamma),H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}))$,
supp$(\gamma_{0}^{\ast}\phi)=\Gamma$, and by Lemma \ref{Lemma_R_k_analytic},
\[
\mathbb{C}\ni\kappa\mapsto 
\begin{bmatrix}
1_{U_{2}}R_{\kappa}1_{\Omega}^{\ast} & 1_{U_{2}}S\!L_{\kappa} 
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is a $\mathscr{B}(H^{-1/2}(\Gamma),,H^{1}(U_{2}))$-valued analytic map.
Similarly,
\[
\mathbb{C}\ni\kappa\mapsto 
\begin{bmatrix}
(cd-1)\Delta_{\Omega}^{\mathrm{max}}1_{\Omega}R_{\kappa}1_{U_{1}}^{\ast}\\
\mu(  d)  \,\gamma_{1}R_{\kappa}1_{U_{1}}^{\ast} 
\end{bmatrix}
\]
is a $\mathscr{B}(L^{2}(U_{1}),H^{-1/2}(\Gamma))$-valued analytic map. Hence,
by Theorem \ref{Theorem_Q_full}, the r.h.s. of (\ref{Krein_EM_cut}) is a
$\mathscr{B}(L^{2}(U_{1}),H^{1}(U_{2}))$-valued meromorphic map. This coincides
with the l.h.s. of (\ref{Krein_EM_cut}) by (\ref{Krein_EM}) and by unique
meromorphic continuation principle.

label: rem-res
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem-res} Notice that there are no $\kappa\in\mathbb R\backslash\{0\}$ such that $\ker(  Q_{\kappa}(
c,d))  \neq\{  0\}$. Indeed, such poles of $\kappa\mapsto Q_{\kappa}(
c,d)$ should correspond to strictly positive isolated eigenvalues of $L_{c,d}$. This is forbidden by $\sigma_{p}(L_{cd})\cap(0,+\infty)=\varnothing$ (see Theorem \ref{theorem_spectrum}). Furthermore, the poles in $\mathbb C_{+}$ of $\kappa\mapsto Q_{\kappa_{\circ}}(c,d)$  correspond to the isolated negative eigenvalues of $L_{c,d}$.
Hence, if $\kappa_{\circ}\in\{\mathbb C\backslash\{0\}:\ker(Q_{\kappa}(c,d))\not=\{0\}\}$ then $\kappa^{2}_{\circ}$ is either a resonance 
or a negative eigenvalue.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Psi\equiv\left(  u,\varphi\right)  $; then: $\Psi\in X_{\circ}$ if and only
if 
\begin{align*}
&  \left.  0=\left\langle \Psi_{\circ},\Psi\right\rangle _{X}=\frac{1}{\lambda
_{\circ}g_{0}}\left\langle D\!L_{0}S_{0}\varphi_{\circ},u\right\rangle _{\Omega
}+\left\langle S_{0}\varphi_{\circ},\varphi\right\rangle _{\Gamma}=\right. \\
&  \left.  \frac{1}{\lambda_{\circ}g_{0}}\left\langle S_{0}\varphi_{\circ},\gamma
_{1}^{\mathrm{in}}N_{0}u\right\rangle _{\Gamma}+\left\langle S_{0}\varphi
_{\circ},\varphi\right\rangle _{\Gamma}=\left\langle S_{0}\varphi_{\circ} 
,\varphi+\frac{1}{\lambda_{\circ}g_{0}}\gamma_{1}^{\mathrm{in}}N_{0}u\right\rangle
_{\Gamma}\,,\right.
\end{align*}
and hence, if and only if 
\[
\pi_{\circ}\left(  \varphi+\frac{1}{\lambda_{\circ}g_{0}}\gamma_{1}^{\mathrm{in}} 
N_{0}u\right)  =0\,.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $u=S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}$; then 
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}
[c]{l} 
-\Delta u=0\,,\qquad\text{in }\Omega\,,\\
\gamma_{0}^{\mathrm{in}}u=S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\,.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
From \cite[Theorem 7.5]{McLe} follows 
\[
u=-DL_{0}S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}+S\!L_{0}S_{0}^{-1}\left(  \frac{1}{2}+N\!P_{0}\right)
S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}\,.
\]
From $N\!P_{0}S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}=\lambda_{\circ}S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}$ follows 
\[
S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}=-DL_{0}S_{0}\varphi_{\circ}+\left(  \frac{1}{2}+\lambda
_{\circ}\right)  S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ} 
\]
where, by \emph{H2}, $\lambda_{\circ}\in\left(  -1/2,1/2\right)  \backslash
\left\{  0\right\}  $. Therefore, we get 
\[
S\!L_{0}\varphi_{\circ}=-\left(  \frac{1}{2}-\lambda_{\circ}\right)  ^{-1}DL_{0} 
S_{0}\varphi_{\circ} 
\]
which corresponds to (\ref{SL_0_id}).

label: Teo-res
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Teo-res}
There exists $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ and a unique couple of
functions $(0,\varepsilon_{0})\ni\varepsilon\mapsto\kappa_{\pm}(  \varepsilon)  $, analytic with respect to  $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$, 
\begin{equation}\label{k_plusmin_exp}
\kappa_{\pm}(\varepsilon)=\pm z_{0}\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,(1+O(  \varepsilon))\pm \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\xi(\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,)\,,\qquad |\xi(t)|\lesssim |t|^{3}
\end{equation}
such that
$$
\ker(Q_{\kappa_{\pm}(\varepsilon)}(\varepsilon))\not=\{0\}\,.
$$
Here, $\pm z_{0}$ are the two roots of the equation
$$
\frac{z^{2}}2+\frac{\rho_{0}}{\lambda_{\circ}}\left\Vert \varphi
_{\circ}\right\Vert _{\hat{H}^{-1/2}(  \Gamma)  }^{2}=0\,.
$$

label: f-g
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\left(  t,z\right)  $ be such that $\left(  t^{2},tz\right)  \in W_{0}$
and define
\begin{equation}\label{f-g}
g(t,z):=t^{-2}f(t^{2},tz)\,.
\end{equation}
By (\ref{f_exp}), there follows 
\[
g\left(  t,z\right)  =c_{1,0}+\frac{1}{2}c_{2,0}t^{2}+\frac{1}{2} 
c_{0,2}\,z^{2}+\frac{1}{6}c_{1,2}\,t^{2}z^{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(  t^{4}\right)
+\mathcal{O}\left(  t^{2}(t^{2}+z^{2})^{2}\right)
\]
and $g$ is analytic. Let 
$$
z_{\pm}=\pm z_{0}\,,\qquad z_{0}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{2\,|c_{1,0}|}&c_{1,0}<0\\
i\sqrt{2\,c_{1,0}}&c_{1,0}>0\,,
\end{cases}
$$
 be the two roots of the equation
\[
c_{1,0}+\frac{1}{2}\,z^{2}=0\,.
\]
One has
$$
g(0,z_{\pm})=0\,,\qquad\partial_{z}g(0,z_{\pm})=c_{0,2}\,z_{\pm} 
\not =0\,,\qquad
$$
$$
\partial_{t}g(0,z_{\pm})=0\,,\qquad\partial_{t}^{2}g(0,z_{\pm
})=c_{2,0}+\frac{1}{3}\,c_{1,2}\,z_{\pm}^{2}=c_{2,0}-\frac{2}{3} 
\,c_{1,0}c_{1,2}\,.
$$
By the implicit function theorem, there exists two unique analytic functions
$$
t\mapsto z_{\pm}(t)=z_{\pm}-\frac{\partial_{t}^{2}g(0,z_{\pm})} 
{2\partial_{z}g(0,z_{\pm})}\,t^{2}+\xi_{\pm }(t)\,,\qquad |\xi_{\pm }(t)|\lesssim |t|^{3}\,,
$$
such that
\[
g(t,z_{\pm}(t))=0\,.
\]
By $g(-t,z)=g(t,-z)$, one has $g(t,-z_{\pm}(-t))=0$ and so, by $z_{\pm}(0)=\pm z_{0}$ and by unicity, one gets
$$
z_{-}(t)=-z_{+}(-t)\,.
$$
Therefore, 
$$
z_{\pm}(t)=\pm z(\pm t)\,,
$$
where
\begin{align*}
  z(t)=&z_{0}\left(  1-\frac{1}{2c_{2,0}z_{0}^{2}}\left(
c_{2,0}-\frac{2}{3}\,c_{1,0}c_{1,2}\right)  t^{2}\right)  +\xi(t)\\
  =&z_{0}\left(  1+\frac{1}{4c_{2,0}c_{1,0}}\left(  c_{2,0}-\frac
{2}{3}\,c_{1,0}c_{1,2}\right)  t^{2}\right)  +\xi(t)\\
 =&z_{0}\left(  1-\frac{1}{4}\left(  \frac{1}{c_{1,0}}-\frac{2} 
{3}\,\frac{c_{1,2}}{c_{2,0}}\right)  t^{2}\right)  +\xi(t)\,,\qquad |\xi(t)|\lesssim |t|^{3}\,.
\end{align*}
By \eqref{f-g},  for $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small,
\[
k_{\pm}(\varepsilon)=\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}z(\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,)=\pm z_{0} 
\sqrt{\varepsilon}\left(  1-\frac{1}{4}\left(  \frac{1}{c_{1,0}}-\frac{2} 
{3}\,\frac{c_{1,2}}{c_{2,0}}\right)  \varepsilon\right)  \pm\sqrt\varepsilon \,\xi(\pm\sqrt\varepsilon\,)
\]
solves
\[
f(\varepsilon,k_{\pm}(\varepsilon))=0\,.
\]

label: Rem-res
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{Rem-res}
Case 1) If $\rho_{0}/\lambda_{\circ}<0$ then 
$$
\kappa_{\pm}(\varepsilon)=
\pm \sqrt{2}\,\left|{\rho_{0}}/
\lambda_{\circ}\right|^{1/2} \|\varphi_{\circ}\| _{\hat{H}^{-1/2}(
\Gamma)  }\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,(1+O(  \varepsilon))\pm \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\xi(\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,)
$$
Case 2) If $\rho_{0}/\lambda_{\circ}>0$ then 
$$
\kappa_{\pm}(\varepsilon)=
\pm i\sqrt{2}\,\left({\rho_{0}}/
\lambda_{\circ}\right)^{1/2} \|\varphi_{\circ}\| _{\hat{H}^{-1/2}(
\Gamma)  }\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,(1+O(  \varepsilon))\pm \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\xi(\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,)
$$
We take in account Remark \ref{rem-res}. In Case 1, since there are no positive eigenvalues, both $\kappa^{2}_{\pm}(\varepsilon)$ are resonances.
In Case 2, $\kappa^{2}_{-}(\varepsilon)$ is a resonance and $\kappa^{2}_{+}(\varepsilon)$ is a negative eigenvalue. Hence, one has the following scenery:

\item{case $\lambda_{\circ}>0$)}  the shift of  $\widetilde d^{-1}$ from $\lambda_{\circ}$ to the right ($\rho_{0}<0$)  generates two branches of resonances,  emanating from the zero eigenvalue. Conversely, the shift of  $\widetilde d^{-1}$ from $\lambda_{\circ}$ to the left ($\rho_{0}>0$)  generates two branches, one consisting of negative eigenvalues and the other of resonances. 

\item{case $\lambda_{\circ}<0$)} the previous results are reversed: the shift to the left   generates two branches of resonances and the shift to the right generates one branch consisting of negative eigenvalues and another one consisting of resonances.
\vskip5pt\noindent
Summing up: if $\widetilde d^{-1}(\varepsilon)/\lambda_{\circ}>1$, then two branches of resonances are created. Otherwise,  if $\widetilde d^{-1}(\varepsilon)/\lambda_{\circ}<1$,  then two branches, one consisting of negative eigenvalues and the other of resonances, are created.
